claims.text: Vascular testing may include MRA, CTA, carotid and transcranial duplex ultrasound and conventional angiography; carotid ultrasound shows the anterior circulation, but MRA and CTA image the posterior circulation better; in general, CTA is preferred to MRA
claims.quote: For vascular causes, testing may include magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), CT angiography (CTA), carotid and transcranial duplex ultrasound, and conventional angiography. The choice and sequence of testing is individualized, based on clinical findings. MRA, CTA, and carotid ultrasound all show the anterior circulation; however, MRA and CTA provide better images of the posterior circulation than carotid ultrasound. In general, CTA is preferred to MRA because motion artifacts are avoided.

claims.text: All patients who have had a TIA require CTA, MRA or diffusion-weighted MRI of the carotid and cerebral circulation
claims.quote: All patients who have had a TIA require CT angiography, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), or diffusion-weighted MRI of the carotid and cerebral circulation.

claims.text: TIA evaluation includes tests for carotid stenosis, cardiac sources of emboli, atrial fibrillation and hematologic abnormalities; stroke risk is highest in the first 24 to 48 hours, so patients are typically admitted
claims.quote: The causes of a TIA are the same as causes of ischemic strokes; evaluation includes tests for carotid stenosis, cardiac sources of emboli, atrial fibrillation, and hematologic abnormalities and screening for stroke risk factors. Because risk of subsequent ischemic stroke is high and immediate, evaluation proceeds rapidly, usually on an inpatient basis. It is not clear which patients, if any, can be safely discharged from the emergency department. Risk of stroke after TIA or minor stroke is highest within the first 24 to 48 hours, so if either is suspected, patients are typically admitted to the hospital for telemetry and evaluation.

claims.text: Causes Most TIAs are caused by emboli, usually from the carotid or vertebral arteries
claims.quote: Most TIAs are caused by emboli, usually from carotid or vertebral arteries, although most causes of ischemic stroke can also result in TIAs.

claims.text: A TIA is focal brain ischemia causing sudden, transient neurologic deficits without permanent infarction
claims.quote: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is focal brain ischemia that causes sudden, transient neurologic deficits and is not accompanied by permanent brain infarction (eg, negative results on diffusion-weighted MRI).

claims.text: Symptoms Deficits are similar to strokes; transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), usually < 5 minutes, may occur when the ophthalmic artery is affected
claims.quote: Neurologic deficits are similar to those of strokes (see table Selected Stroke Syndromes). Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), which usually lasts < 5 minutes, may occur when the ophthalmic artery is affected.

claims.text: Symptoms begin suddenly, usually last 2 to 30 minutes, then resolve completely; successive carotid attacks are usually similar
claims.quote: Symptoms of TIAs begin suddenly, usually last 2 to 30 minutes, then resolve completely. Patients may have several TIAs daily or only 2 or 3 over several years. Symptoms are usually similar in successive carotid attacks but vary somewhat in successive vertebrobasilar attacks.

claims.text: A TIA is diagnosed retrospectively when the deficits resolve within 1 hour
claims.quote: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is diagnosed retrospectively when sudden neurologic deficits referable to ischemia in an arterial territory resolve within 1 hour.

claims.text: Endarterectomy or stenting after a recent nondisabling stroke from ipsilateral carotid obstruction of 70 to 99% (or an ulcerated plaque) with life expectancy ≥ 5 years; other symptomatic patients (eg, TIAs): endarterectomy or stenting plus antiplatelet therapy for obstruction ≥ 60%, if life expectancy is at least 5 years
claims.quote: Extracranial carotid endarterectomy or stenting is indicated for patients with recent nondisabling, submaximal stroke attributed to an ipsilateral carotid obstruction of 70 to 99% of the arterial lumen or to an ulcerated plaque if life expectancy is at least 5 years. In other symptomatic patients (eg, patients with TIAs), endarterectomy or stenting combined with antiplatelet therapy is indicated for carotid obstruction of ≥ 60% with or without ulceration if life expectancy is at least 5 years.

claims.text: TIA treatment aims to prevent stroke: antiplatelets and statins; endarterectomy or angioplasty plus stenting can be useful for some, particularly those at high risk (> 70% ipsilateral carotid stenosis); anticoagulation if there is a cardiac source of emboli
claims.quote: Treatment of transient ischemic attacks is aimed at preventing strokes; antiplatelet medications and statins are used. Carotid endarterectomy or arterial angioplasty plus stenting can be useful for some patients, particularly those who have no neurologic deficits but who are at high risk of stroke (> 70% ipsilateral carotid stenosis). Anticoagulation is indicated if cardiac sources of emboli are present.
